paperTitle: Singapore-Cambridge GCE O-Level 1184 English Language — AI-authored Simplified Practice 40: The New Glasses (§B style, simplified band)

sections.instruction: Read the narrative text below and answer the questions that follow. Section B, Part 1 [11 marks]. Answer in your own words as far as possible.
sections.passage:
Paragraph 1
For most of Primary Five I had been squinting at the whiteboard, screwing up my eyes until the words swam into something I could almost read, and copying the rest from the girl beside me. I thought everybody saw the world that way. It was my form teacher who noticed, and after the eye test at the polyclinic the optician told my mother, quite cheerfully, that I would need glasses.

Paragraph 2
I did not want them. In my class only one boy wore glasses, and some of the others had a name for him that they thought was funny. I pictured myself walking into the classroom with two circles of glass on my face and everybody turning to look. I told my mother I could see the board perfectly well. She listened, and then she bought the glasses anyway.

Paragraph 3
On the first morning I kept them zipped inside my pencil case until the bell had gone and everyone was seated. Only then did I take them out and put them on. They perched on my nose, strange and heavy, and the whole room seemed to tip for a second before it settled.

Paragraph 4
Behind me, a boy laughed and said something to his friend, and the two of them looked at me. My ears went hot. I stared down at my desk and pretended to hunt for something in my bag, wishing the floor would open.

Paragraph 5
Then my teacher began writing on the board, and I read every word of it from where I sat, without leaning forward once. At recess I stood at the corridor window and looked out at the big rain tree in the field. It was not a soft green cloud any more. It was a thousand separate leaves, every one of them edged and sharp, moving on their own in the wind. I stood there until the bell rang and I still had not finished looking.

Paragraph 6
After that I stopped putting the glasses away. When my teacher asked a question about something on the board, mine was the first hand up, because for the first time I could actually read it. I began to answer without checking first with the girl beside me.

Paragraph 7
The boy behind me kept up his jokes for about a week, and then he found something else to laugh at. By then I had stopped minding very much. He could say what he liked; I could see the leaves on the rain tree, and that turned out to matter a great deal more.

(Glossary: Primary Five: the fifth year of primary school in Singapore; polyclinic: a government-run neighbourhood health centre; rain tree: a large, broad-crowned tree commonly planted along Singapore roads and fields.)

questions.stem: Q1. In Paragraph 1, what TWO things did the narrator do in order to keep up in class? [1]
questions.answer: she screwed up her eyes / squinted to try to make out the words, and copied the rest from the girl beside her. EITHER point alone earns the mark.

questions.stem: Q2. What does the phrase 'the words swam' (Paragraph 1) suggest about how the whiteboard looked to the narrator? [1]
questions.answer: the writing looked blurred and unsteady, seeming to shift or float so that it could not be read clearly

questions.stem: Q3. What does the word 'perched' in 'They perched on my nose' (Paragraph 3) suggest about how the glasses sat? [1]
questions.answer: that they sat up on the bridge of the nose, resting there rather than feeling part of the narrator — as if they might easily slip off. Accept 'balanced on the nose, as if it could slide off' or 'did not yet feel like part of her'. REJECT a bare 'sat on the nose' (no understanding shown), and REJECT 'lightly' — the same sentence says they felt 'strange and heavy'.

questions.stem: Q4. Using your own words, explain why the narrator did not want to wear glasses. (Paragraph 2) [2]
questions.answer: MP1 (fear of being mocked): the only boy in her class who wore glasses was given an unkind nickname, so she expected the same treatment; MP2 (fear of being stared at): she imagined walking in with glasses on her face and the whole class turning to look at her, which she dreaded. Award one mark per distinct point.

questions.stem: Q5. In Paragraph 3 the narrator puts the glasses on for the first time. Using your own words, describe TWO ways in which wearing them felt unfamiliar. [2]
questions.answer: MP1 (how they felt on the face): they were odd and heavy sitting on the nose — they did not yet feel like a natural part of her; MP2 (what they did to her view): the whole room seemed to tip or swim for a moment before it settled, so even her sense of the space around her was disturbed. Award one mark per distinct point. NOTE for markers: 'she did not want to be seen wearing them' belongs to Q4 — do NOT award it here.

questions.stem: Q6. Using your own words, explain why the narrator 'had stopped minding very much' about the boy's jokes. (Paragraphs 6-7) [2]
questions.answer: MP1 (something better outweighs it): being able to see properly — reading the board, seeing the leaves on the rain tree — mattered far more to the narrator than the teasing did, so the jokes lost their power; MP2 (no longer dependent on others): she could now answer in class first, without copying or checking with the girl beside her, so she no longer needed the other pupils' approval and could let the boy 'say what he liked'. Award one mark per distinct point. REJECT 'because the boy stopped teasing her' — 'By then' shows she had already stopped minding before he found something else to laugh at.

questions.stem: Q7. What is the effect of describing the rain tree as no longer 'a soft green cloud' but 'a thousand separate leaves, every one of them edged and sharp' (Paragraph 5)? [2]
questions.answer: the contrast between a vague, shapeless mass and countless precisely-defined leaves dramatises just how much detail her poor eyesight had hidden from her, making the moment of seeing clearly feel like a discovery of a whole new world

sections.instruction: Q8. [4 marks in total] The narrator's main feeling changes as the story goes on. For each moment below, go back to the relevant paragraphs of the narrative and choose ONE word from the bank that best describes her dominant feeling there. Some words in the bank are not used, and each word may be used once only. Word bank: amazed / angry / bored / confident / embarrassed / jealous / reluctant / sleepy.
sections.passage: Refer to the same 'The New Glasses' narrative in Exercise 1 above. Read the paragraphs named in each question, then choose the single word from the bank that best describes how the narrator feels at that moment.
